To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) i-voting intent has a positive impact on voting intent, 2) the performance expectation, the perception on ease of user and the trust in the internet have a positive impact on i-voting intent, while the trust in the government has a negative impact, and 3) i-voting intention is positively influenced by the perception of i-voting, and the trust in internet and government.

the performance expectation, perception of ease of use, and trust in the Internet are positively associated with on-line voting intent, and that on-line voting intent is a positive predictor of intent to vote.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the introduction of on-line voting could boost voting intention.
the relationship between on-line voting and intent to vote.
the relationship of the technology acceptance model and the intent to vote.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
on-line voting is a feasible and desirable option in Hungary, and the key factors to increase on-line voting intent are performance expectation, perception of ease of use and internet trust.
on-line voting is a feasible and acceptable solution to boost voting participation amongst young Hungarian citizens.
on-line voting could be a powerful tool to boost the desire of young Hungarian citizens to vote.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
on-line voting is perceived as an effective tool to enhance democratic participation amongst young Hungarian voters.
the more young Hungarian citizens perceive on-line voting as an easy and useful tool for voting, the more likely they will vote.
our results indicate that young, educated and Internet-ready Hungarian citizens are willing to use on-line voting system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
on-line voting could be a viable option to boost voting rates among the young and the educated.
the technology acceptance perceptions of young, educated, and internet-ready voters in the CEE region are not the same as those in the West.
the internet is a tool that can be used to increase voter turnout.
